title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: "I now come to the more moving part of my story. I'll describe events that transformed me from what I was into what I am.

"Spring advanced quickly. The weather turned fine and the skies cleared. I was surprised that what had been so barren and gloomy now bloomed with the most beautiful flowers and greenery. My senses were refreshed by a thousand delightful scents and a thousand lovely sights.

"It was on one of those days when the cottagers rested from work — the old man played his guitar while the children listened — that I noticed Felix looked deeply melancholy. He sighed frequently. Once his father paused his music, and I guessed from his manner that he was asking about his son's sadness. Felix replied cheerfully, and the old man was starting his music again when someone knocked at the door.

"It was a lady on horseback, accompanied by a country man as a guide. She wore a dark outfit and was covered with a thick black veil. Agatha asked a question. The stranger replied only by pronouncing, in a sweet accent, the name of Felix. Her voice was musical but different from either of my friends'. Hearing this name, Felix rushed to the lady. When she saw him, she threw up her veil, and I saw a face of angelic beauty. Her hair was shining black and intricately braided. Her eyes were dark but gentle and lively. Her features were perfectly proportioned. Her complexion was wonderfully fair, each cheek touched with a lovely pink.

"Felix seemed overwhelmed with joy when he saw her. Every trace of sorrow vanished from his face, replaced by an ecstatic happiness I could hardly have imagined. His eyes sparkled. His cheeks flushed with pleasure. At that moment I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She seemed to feel differently. Wiping tears from her lovely eyes, she offered her hand to Felix. He kissed it rapturously and called her — as far as I could make out — his sweet Arabian. She didn't seem to understand him, but smiled. He helped her dismount. After dismissing her guide, he led her into the cottage. Some conversation took place between Felix and his father. The young stranger knelt at the old man's feet and would have kissed his hand, but he raised her up and embraced her warmly.

"I soon noticed that although the stranger spoke and seemed to have her own language, she couldn't understand the cottagers, nor they her. They made many gestures I didn't understand, but her presence clearly brought joy to the cottage, banishing their sadness the way the sun clears morning mist. Felix seemed especially happy, welcoming his Arabian with beaming smiles. Agatha, ever gentle, kissed the stranger's hands and pointed to her brother, making signs that seemed to mean he'd been sad until she came. Several hours passed this way. The cause of their happiness escaped me, but I could see it on their faces. Then I noticed the stranger was trying to learn their language, repeating sounds they said to her. The idea instantly struck me that I could use the same lessons. The stranger learned about twenty words in the first session. Most were ones I already knew, but I benefited from the rest.

"As night came, Agatha and the Arabian retired early. When they parted, Felix kissed the stranger's hand and said, 'Good night, sweet Safie.' He stayed up much longer talking with his father. From the frequent mention of her name, I guessed their lovely guest was the subject of their conversation. I desperately wanted to understand them, but found it completely impossible.

"The next morning, Felix went to work. After Agatha finished her usual tasks, the Arabian sat at the old man's feet. Taking his guitar, she played music so hauntingly beautiful that it drew tears of both sorrow and joy from my eyes. She sang, and her voice flowed in rich waves, swelling or dying away like a nightingale in the woods.

"When she finished, she gave the guitar to Agatha, who at first declined it. She played a simple tune and sang in a sweet voice, but without the stranger's extraordinary skill. The old man seemed transported with delight. He said some words that Agatha tried to explain to Safie — apparently expressing how much joy her music brought him.

"The days now passed as peacefully as before, with the only change being that joy had replaced sadness on my friends' faces. Safie was always cheerful. She and I improved rapidly in the language, so that within two months I could understand most of what my protectors said.

"Meanwhile, the black earth was covered with new growth. The green banks were dotted with countless flowers — sweet-scented and beautiful, like pale stars among the moonlit woods. The sun grew warmer. The nights became clear and balmy. My nighttime rambles were a great pleasure, although they were cut short by the late setting and early rising of the sun. I never ventured out during daylight, fearing a repeat of my earlier treatment in the village.

"My days were spent in close study so I could master the language more quickly. I can honestly say I improved faster than the Arabian, who understood very little and spoke in broken fragments, while I could comprehend and imitate nearly every word.
"While I improved in speech, I also learned the science of reading, as it was taught to the stranger. This opened a vast new world of wonder and delight.

"The book Felix used to teach Safie was Volney's _Ruins of Empires_. I wouldn't have understood it if Felix hadn't provided very detailed explanations as he read. He'd chosen this work, he said, because its grand, declamatory style was modeled on Eastern authors. Through this book I gained a basic knowledge of history and an overview of the world's empires. I learned about the manners, governments, and religions of different nations. I heard about the lazy Asiatics, the stupendous genius of the Greeks, the wars and extraordinary virtue of the early Romans — their later decline and the fall of that mighty empire — chivalry, Christianity, and kings. I heard about the discovery of the Americas and wept with Safie over the tragic fate of the native peoples.

"These wonderful stories stirred strange feelings in me. Was man really at once so powerful, so virtuous and magnificent, yet so vicious and base? He appeared at one moment a mere offshoot of evil, and at another the noblest, most godlike being imaginable. Being a great and virtuous person seemed the highest honor a conscious being could achieve. Being base and vicious, as many people in history have been, seemed the lowest degradation — worse than a blind mole or harmless worm. For a long time I couldn't understand how one person could go out and murder another, or even why there were laws and governments. But when I heard the details of human cruelty and bloodshed, my wonder ceased. I turned away with disgust and horror.

"Every conversation in the cottage now opened new wonders for me. From Felix's lessons to the Arabian, I learned about the strange system of human society — the division of property, immense wealth alongside crushing poverty, rank, bloodlines, and noble birth.

"These words forced me to look at myself. I learned that what your fellow creatures valued most was high, pure ancestry combined with wealth. A man might be respected with just one of these, but without either he was considered — with rare exceptions — a vagrant and a slave, doomed to waste his abilities for the benefit of the privileged few! And what was I? I knew absolutely nothing about my creation or creator. I had no money, no friends, no property of any kind. I was also endowed with a hideously deformed and loathsome body. I wasn't even the same kind of being as man. I was more agile than they were and could survive on rougher food. I endured extremes of heat and cold with less harm. I was far taller than any human. When I looked around, I saw and heard of no one like me. Was I, then, a monster? A stain upon the earth, from which all men fled and which all men rejected?

"I can't describe the agony these thoughts caused me. I tried to push them away, but sorrow only grew with knowledge. Oh, if only I had stayed forever in my native forest, never knowing or feeling anything beyond hunger, thirst, and warmth!

"What a strange thing knowledge is! Once it takes hold of the mind, it clings like lichen on rock. I sometimes wished I could shake off all thought and feeling. But I learned there was only one way to overcome pain, and that was death — a state I feared but didn't understand. I admired virtue and good feeling. I loved the gentle manners and kind qualities of my cottagers. But I was shut out from any real connection with them, except through the stolen, secret glimpses I took when unseen and unknown — and these only increased my longing to be one of them. Agatha's gentle words and the charming Arabian's bright smiles were not for me. The old man's mild encouragement and Felix's lively conversation were not for me. Miserable, unhappy wretch!

"Other lessons struck me even more deeply. I heard about the differences between the sexes, and the birth and growth of children — how the father doted on the infant's smiles and the older child's playfulness, how the mother's whole life and care wrapped around this precious charge, how the young mind expanded and gained knowledge — of brothers, sisters, and all the various bonds that tie human beings to one another.

"But where were my own family and friends? No father had watched over my infancy. No mother had blessed me with smiles and tenderness. Or if they had, my entire past was a blank, a dark emptiness in which I could make out nothing. From my earliest memory, I'd been as I was now in height and build. I'd never seen anyone who resembled me or claimed any connection with me. What was I? The question kept returning, answered only by groans.

"I'll soon explain where these feelings led. But first, let me return to the cottagers, whose story stirred such varied feelings in me — outrage, delight, and wonder — all of which ended in deeper love and reverence for my protectors (for so I loved, in an innocent, half-painful self-deception, to call them)."
